week.t: NASA: applications open for the next astronaut class; US citizens have until 3 December
Science News Explores: a model for why ant colonies burst into activity with no leader
NTU: evidence of hydrogen atoms inside a metal’s crystal lattice, after a plunge to −196°C
Hubble: image of Messier 30, a globular cluster 27,500 light-years away, released 5 November
Physics World: when two people see a screen’s colours differently, the display can be the cause
PIB: JNCASR silicon chip carries 100 Gbit/s across a terahertz barrier with 1–2% loss

tiles.cap: NASA is hiring astronauts. Last time, more than 8,000 people applied and 10 got in
tiles.nums: applicants were chosen for NASA’s 2025 astronaut class; applications for the next class opened on Saturday
tiles.p1: NASA opened applications on Saturday 7 November for its next class of astronauts, who it says will join the agency as America returns to the Moon, builds the Moon Base and lays the groundwork for the first crewed missions to Mars. US citizens have until 11:59 pm US Eastern on Thursday 3 December to submit their applications, and NASA expects to make its final selection in late 2027. The agency last opened applications in 2024: from more than 8,000 applications, 10 astronaut candidates were selected in 2025 and are now completing nearly two years of training.
tiles.p2: Why this weekend: the call went out during NASA’s MAX POWER events in Florida, which run from Friday 6 to Sunday 8 November and include a Moon Base news conference at 5 pm US Eastern on Saturday, 6 am on Sunday in Singapore.
deep: The numbers
Since the 1960s, NASA has selected 370 people to train as astronaut candidates. The agency has 32 astronauts active in its astronaut corps today.
If you want to fly it

For pilots, NASA lists 750 hours as pilot in command of high-performance jet aircraft, or 1,500 total flight hours in other fixed-wing aircraft including 750 as pilot in command, or 1,000 total flight hours in rotary-wing aircraft including 300 as pilot in command. Only US citizens can apply.
What they said

“This is an extraordinary time to join NASA’s astronaut corps,” said NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman, adding that the missions “will demand technical excellence, sound judgment, teamwork, and courage.” Deputy Administrator Matt Anderson put it shorter: “The window is open. The mission is waiting.”
Who picks

Scott Tingle, chief astronaut, chairs the Astronaut Selection Board at NASA’s Johnson Space Center in Houston; for those who apply, he says, becoming a NASA astronaut “is more than a career opportunity”. The photo shows NASA announcing its 2025 astronaut candidate class at Johnson on 22 September 2025.
tiles.src: NASA news release 26-093, 7 Nov 2026 · NASA media advisory M26-084 (MAX POWER key events), updated 2 Nov 2026

tiles.cap: This ball of stars orbits our galaxy the wrong way. The Milky Way may have captured it
tiles.nums: to Messier 30, a globular cluster in Capricornus, in a Hubble image released on 5 November
tiles.p1: Messier 30 is a globular cluster: a roughly spherical grouping of stars containing anywhere from tens of thousands to millions of stars, lying about 27,500 light-years away in the constellation Capricornus. Our Milky Way galaxy has at least 150 globular clusters, the nearest about 6,000 light-years away. Astronomers estimate their ages at between 11.5 and 13.5 billion years, which makes certain globular clusters nearly as old as the universe itself.
tiles.p2: The twist: researchers have discovered that M30 and many other globular clusters orbit in the direction opposite to the way our galaxy spins. Instead of forming with the Milky Way, they may have been captured by it in the distant past.
deep: Named for a comet hunter
The sparkling collection of stars is named Messier 30 after the French astronomer Charles Messier. It is also catalogued as NGC 7099.
Fifteen years of watching

Hubble first observed these stars 15 years ago, and comparing positions across that time lets astronomers measure how the stars move. An earlier Hubble survey of the cluster, in red and near-infrared light, revealed stars down to just 20 per cent of the mass of the Sun.
How we found our place
More than a century ago, the astronomer Harlow Shapley used observations of a particular type of variable star in globular clusters. His work showed that the Sun is not in the centre of our galaxy.
tiles.src: NASA Science, Hubble: “Hubble Learns Galactic History From Stars”, 5 Nov 2026 · NASA image article “M30’s Sparkling Stars”, 6 Nov 2026
tiles.credit: Photo: ESA/Hubble & NASA, M. Libralato, G. Piotto, A. Sarajedini

tiles.cap: Two fridge-sized probes slingshot past Earth: one Saturday, the second Monday 7 pm here
tiles.nums: the length of each trans-Mars injection burn, adding more than 1,000 mph (about 1,600 km/h)
tiles.p1: NASA’s twin ESCAPADE spacecraft perform a manoeuvre no agency spacecraft has flown before, a powered flyby of Earth, and do it twice: once for each spacecraft. The first spacecraft’s flyby and roughly 9-minute engine burn were scheduled for around 5 am US Eastern on Saturday 7 November, 6 pm in Singapore; NASA’s ESCAPADE blog had not posted the result when this edition was written early on Sunday. The second spacecraft follows around 6 am Eastern on Monday 9 November, 7 pm here, with its burn starting at 5:51 am Eastern. Each burn is made over southern Australia and raises the craft’s speed from about 6.3 to about 6.7 miles per second (roughly 10.1 to 10.8 km/s).
tiles.p2: Why now: ESCAPADE launched in November 2025 when Earth and Mars were on opposite sides of the Sun, so the pair looped around Earth–Sun Lagrange point 2 in a loiter orbit, waiting for the right moment to be thrown onward.
deep: How close

Closest approach is between 600 and 1,100 miles (roughly 970 to 1,770 km) above the surface. At the speed they leave, NASA says, the spacecraft could fly from Washington, DC, to San Francisco in less than 7 minutes. That is about Mach 31.
Then the long cruise

After the flybys comes a 10-month cruise. Arrival at Mars is set for 7 and 9 September 2027, where the pair will be the first multi-spacecraft mission to fly in formation around the planet, measuring how the solar wind strips away the Martian atmosphere.
Bonus science on the way
While loitering, the spacecraft flew through a distant part of Earth’s magnetotail, the long magnetic wake the solar wind drags out behind our planet. NASA says those findings will be shared soon.
Can you see them
NASA says the spacecraft are faint and a telescope will most likely be needed; the coordinates come from JPL’s Horizons system. Each one is about the size of a standard refrigerator.
tiles.src: NASA ESCAPADE blog, 2 Nov 2026 (Vanessa Thomas, Goddard)

tiles.cap: Mars and Jupiter pass 1.2° apart on 15–16 November, and three supermoons start on the 24th
tiles.nums: Leonid meteors at best, before dawn on 17–18 November, after the Moon has set
tiles.p1: NASA’s What’s Up for November 2026, presented by Raquel Villanueva of JPL: the Southern Taurids peaked around 5 November with occasional bright fireballs; the Northern Taurids follow around the 12th at about five meteors an hour under ideal conditions; Mars and Jupiter appear about 1.2 degrees apart before sunrise on 15–16 November, Jupiter the brighter, Mars reddish; and the Leonids are best before dawn on 17–18 November, up to around 15 an hour under ideal skies.
tiles.p2: Why now: the Southern Taurids peaked around 5 November, the Northern Taurids follow around the 12th, and the full Moon on 24 November is the first of three supermoons in a row.
deep: Moon phases
NASA lists November’s Moon phases in US Pacific Time: third quarter on the 1st, new Moon on the 8th, first quarter on the 17th, full supermoon on the 24th, third quarter again on the 30th.
1.2 degrees
Mars and Jupiter appear about 1.2 degrees apart before sunrise on 15–16 November, Jupiter the brighter and Mars reddish. NASA says both planets are easy to see with the unaided eye.
A light-day away
This month Voyager 1 becomes the first human-made object one light-day from Earth: a signal travelling at the speed of light takes 24 hours to reach it. NASA celebrates on 17 November.
Seeing meteors
NASA’s advice for the Leonids: find a dark location and give your eyes about half an hour to adjust. The hours to try are before dawn on 17–18 November, after the Moon has set.
tiles.src: NASA Science, What’s Up: November 2026 Skywatching Tips (Raquel Villanueva, JPL), 2 Nov 2026

tiles.cap: A Bengaluru chip sends terahertz waves through a barrier with 1–2% loss, at 100 Gbit/s
tiles.nums: carried by the chip’s splitter; at that rate a 5-gigabyte high-definition film could in principle be transferred in under half a second
tiles.p1: Researchers at JNCASR in Bengaluru have made a silicon chip in which terahertz waves pass through an engineered barrier with little loss while carrying data at 100 gigabits per second. A single barrier added only about 1 to 2 per cent loss, and two barriers in sequence about 2 to 3 per cent. Future sixth-generation (6G) wireless networks are expected to use terahertz frequencies, and the work points to compact terahertz circuits for them.
tiles.p2: Why here: two of the collaborators, Zhonghua Gu and Prakash Pitchappa, are at the Institute of Microelectronics at A*STAR in Singapore. The paper is in Advanced Materials, and the release came from India’s Ministry of Science and Technology on 4 November.
deep: Three devices

The concept was tested in three devices fabricated on high-resistivity silicon, including one with an omega-shaped route containing four sharp bends and a central barrier. Measurements across 310 to 360 GHz agreed closely with simulations.
The data runs

In high-speed tests the double-barrier and omega-shaped devices carried 48 and 60 Gbit/s. The splitter supported 100 Gbit/s using QAM-32 modulation, which encodes information in the signal’s amplitude and phase.
Who

The work was led by Dr Abhishek Kumar, Assistant Professor at JNCASR, who heads its Meta Optics Laboratory (MetoLab), with Samina Mulla and Sangram Kumar Sadhu of JNCASR as joint first authors. Collaborators include IISER Kolkata, IIT Bombay, A*STAR, and the University of Lille and CNRS in France.
The idea

The release describes the effect as photonic Klein tunnelling: the barrier is created simply by changing the geometry of the holes in the chip. Dr Kumar said the result “suggests that this effect can become a useful design tool for terahertz chips”.
tiles.src: PIB, Ministry of Science & Technology, release of 4 Nov 2026 (PRID 2332613) · Advanced Materials, DOI 10.1002/adma.75322
tiles.credit: Photo: PIB / JNCASR (the MetoLab team with the chip)

tiles.cap: Hydrogen hides in metal and snaps it. NTU froze an alloy to −196°C and caught it in place
tiles.nums: the liquid nitrogen the specimen was plunged into, to slow the hydrogen down enough to catch it
tiles.p1: Hydrogen atoms that dissolve into a metal’s crystal lattice can make it brittle, and the failures can be sudden: NTU cites a Boeing 737 that lost a nose wheel at Melbourne Airport in 2009 and 32 steel anchor rods that fractured during construction of the San Francisco–Oakland Bay Bridge in 2013. A team led by Nanyang Assistant Professor Eason Chen of NTU’s School of Materials Science and Engineering has now obtained evidence of hydrogen dissolved in a metal’s crystal lattice, using cryogenic atom probe tomography on a high-entropy alloy. The findings are published in Nature.
tiles.p2: Why it was hard: “The existence of hydrogen in materials is a bit like the existence of black holes,” says Chen. “We know it’s there, but it’s very difficult to observe.”
deep: The trick

The specimen was plunged into liquid nitrogen at −196°C to slow the hydrogen’s movement. “The challenge was finding a material that could hold onto the hydrogen long enough for us to measure it,” says collaborator Dr Shi Rongjian.
Why it matters

Hydrogen embrittlement is the name for this weakening, and the nose wheel and the bridge rods are the two examples NTU gives. Seeing where the hydrogen sits, atom by atom, is the starting point for alloys that resist it.
Who
Chen joined NTU in 2024. His doctoral research was at the University of Oxford in 2014, and he set up a US$3 million programme at the University of Sydney before coming to Singapore.
tiles.src: NTU College of Engineering news, “In Pursuit of Hydrogen”, 5 Nov 2026 (Laura Dobberstein) · Nature

tiles.cap: A*STAR’s automated lab screens up to 470 alloys a day, over 400 times the usual rate
tiles.nums: unique alloy samples screened and tested by MARVEL-AI’s metals line, more than 400 times conventional throughput
tiles.p1: MARVEL-AI is an A*STAR-led initiative that links AI prediction, automated experiments and testing in a loop, with each round’s results feeding the next. It covers four classes of materials: metal alloys, polymers and organics, ceramics, and composites. For alloys, up to 470 unique samples can be screened and tested per day, which A*STAR says is more than 400 times conventional throughput.
tiles.p2: Why now: the initiative was announced on 27 October under Singapore’s RIE2030 research plan, with industry collaborations across aerospace, advanced manufacturing, precision electronics and specialty polymers.
deep: Polymers round the clock

The polymer workflow went from an 8-hour window handling up to 3 samples one after another to 24-hour continuous operation with up to 25 samples in parallel, producing 75 samples in 24 hours, about 25 times the daily output.
A lighter hydrogen capsule
On the composites side, a prototype hydrogen-carrying capsule came out 50 per cent lighter and four times more durable.
Discovery is not enough

“AI is creating unprecedented opportunities for materials discovery, but discovery alone is not enough,” says Professor Loh Xian Jun, Executive Director of MARVEL-AI. “The next challenge is proving they can work in the real world.” Partners include ST Engineering, Foxconn Industrial Internet, Google Cloud and Shimadzu.
tiles.src: A*STAR press release, “MARVEL-AI: Accelerating Advanced Materials Innovation From Discovery To Deployment”, 27 Oct 2026

tiles.cap: Glasses with a 70° view, 1920×1200 per eye, 95 g. The computer lives in your pocket
tiles.nums: for the glasses; the tethered puck that does the computing weighs 265 g and carries a 4,455 mAh battery
tiles.p1: XREAL’s Aura, on TIME’s Best Inventions of 2026 list, puts the computing power in a tethered puck that clips over a pocket or hangs on a lanyard, so the glasses themselves weigh 95 g. Each eye gets a Sony micro-OLED at 1920 × 1200 pixels, up to 120 Hz, with a 70-degree diagonal field of view through XREAL’s X Prism optics and electrochromic dimming in five steps. Three cameras sit on the front frame: two tracking cameras at the corners for hand tracking and spatial anchoring, and one RGB camera with a privacy LED.
tiles.p2: Why now: XREAL says shipping is expected to begin in mid-November 2026, at US$1,099 on its US store, with the US, Canada, Japan and South Korea first.
deep: The puck

It runs Android XR on a Snapdragon platform rated at 48 TOPS of AI processing, with 12 or 16 GB of memory, a fan for cooling and a 4,455 mAh rated battery. It takes Bluetooth keyboards, mice and game controllers, and has a fingerprint button.
Latency
XREAL’s X1S co-processor in the glasses is rated at 3 ms motion-to-photon latency, the delay between your head moving and the picture updating. Brightness is rated up to 1,050 nits.
What reviewers found wrong

Tom’s Guide’s Jason England, trying them at Google I/O in May, saw “some edge blurring”, found it “slower to do things than on an actual computer”, and wrote that “you won’t be taking these outside in public without getting second looks”. He estimated the puck is “probably good for 2-3 hours of heavy use”; XREAL lists no battery life in hours.
The price problem

England: “I’d love for these to be sub-$1,000, I don’t see a world where this happens.” TechRadar’s Hamish Hector, trying them at IFA in September, hoped for the same and noted “there’s only so cheap we can expect XR tech to get”.
tiles.src: TIME Best Inventions 2026 (Richard Eisenberg, 15 Oct 2026) · XREAL Aura specifications and US store · Tom’s Guide hands-on (Jason England, updated 21 May 2026) · TechRadar (Hamish Hector, 4 Sep 2026)

tiles.cap: A full gamepad under an inch thick snaps to your phone by magnet and slides out to play
tiles.nums: its polling rate over a cable, on the maker’s spec sheet; over Bluetooth it is 125 Hz
tiles.p1: TIME’s Best Inventions 2026 list includes the Mcon, a mobile game controller from OhSnap. It attaches to your phone magnetically and pops out to reveal a full-size gamepad with thumbsticks, analog triggers and fold-out grips. A slider mechanism makes it easy to switch back to using the phone for calls and messages, and the controller is less than an inch thick. The maker’s spec sheet puts it at 144.1 × 69.4 × 24.1 mm and 197 g, and lists it at US$149.99.
tiles.p2: Why TIME picked it: “What good is a mobile game controller if it gives you hand cramps?” TIME says the Mcon does not sacrifice functionality for pocketability.
deep: Sticks and triggers

Ohsnap says the joysticks are full-size GameSir “Mag-Res” (TMR) sticks, which it describes as ultra accurate, lower in power consumption and “anti-stick drift”, and as better than Hall-effect ones. The triggers are Hall-effect analog triggers, which the maker says allow precise control in throttle-based games. A gyroscope enables motion-based input for tilt-to-aim, driving or flying games.
Three ways to connect

The spec sheet gives a polling rate for each connection: 125 Hz over Bluetooth Low Energy, 1,000 Hz wired, and 250 to 1,000 Hz over a 2.4 GHz mode that works with the maker’s Dock or Key Cast. The Bluetooth version is 5.4, the stated maximum range is 10 m, and the pad can connect to up to 3 devices and switch between them.
Battery and magnets

Inside is a 500 mAh lithium-ion battery, rated for up to 9 hours of continuous use and up to 1.8 years on standby. Closing the Mcon activates an auto wake/sleep function and protects the controls. It fits MagSafe and PixelSnap phones and cases, with an adapter included for Android phones and regular cases. Your phone can charge the Mcon over USB-C, but the Mcon will not charge your phone.
What a reviewer found wrong

John Velasco of Tom’s Guide tried one, in an article published on 25 August 2026, and liked it: he wrote that it packs all the buttons, triggers, joysticks and grips needed to feel remarkably like a standard console controller. His caveats: much as he appreciates the wireless connection, “there are just some games”, like Resident Evil Village, “that are better suited with a direct connection”, and he gets rid of any worry about latency by connecting it via USB-C. Next to his iPhone 17 Pro it has a nearly identical footprint, “just with a slightly thicker chassis”.
tiles.src: TIME Best Inventions 2026 (Jessica Sager) · Ohsnap MCON product page · Tom’s Guide, 25 Aug 2026 (John Velasco)

tiles.cap: A satellite’s mass grows by one part in two to three billion, Feynman notes. Check his sum
tiles.nums: the normal mass of the electrons in Caltech’s synchrotron, Feynman wrote: as heavy as a proton
tiles.p1: For over 200 years Newton’s equations of motion were believed to describe nature correctly, Feynman writes, and the first time an error in these laws was discovered, the way to correct it was discovered too; both by Einstein in 1905. The fix changes Newton’s laws by introducing a correction factor to the mass, which grows with speed. A satellite goes around the Earth at 5 miles per second, so v/c is 5/186,000, and putting that into the formula shows the correction to the mass is only one part in two to three billion, “which is nearly impossible to observe.”
tiles.p2: Check it: type 5 ÷ 186000 into a calculator, square it, then halve it. You get about 3.6 × 10⁻¹⁰, which is one part in roughly 2.8 billion: the size of the correction Feynman is talking about.
deep: Found on paper first
“Because the effect is ordinarily so small,” Feynman writes, “it seems remarkable that it was discovered theoretically before it was discovered experimentally.”
Where it is huge

To deflect the high-speed electrons in the synchrotron at Caltech, Feynman says, a magnetic field 2000 times stronger than Newton’s laws would predict is needed: the electrons’ mass is 2000 times as great as their normal mass, as great as that of a proton. Yet their speed cannot exceed the speed of light.
Clocks too

Not only must lengths shorten, Feynman writes, but clocks must slow down: when a clock in a space ship records 1 second as seen by the man in the ship, it shows 1/√(1 − u²/c²) second to the man outside.
And energy
Near the chapter’s end comes the famous link: the mass is equal to the total energy content divided by c².
tiles.src: The Feynman Lectures on Physics, Vol. I, Ch. 15 “The Special Theory of Relativity” (sections 15-1, 15-4, 15-8, 15-9), feynmanlectures.caltech.edu

tiles.cap: Sit on a swivel chair holding two water bottles, pull your arms in, and you speed up
tiles.nums: of water in each hand works; the Exploratorium says to use the heaviest masses you can hold at arm’s length
tiles.p1: The Exploratorium’s Momentum Machine needs a rotating stool or chair, two heavy objects such as two 2-litre plastic bottles full of water, and a partner. Sit with one mass in each hand and your arms outstretched, have your partner start you rotating slowly and then let go and move away, and quickly pull the masses in towards your body. You rotate faster.
tiles.p2: Why: a rotating object tends to keep a constant angular momentum unless an outside twisting force acts on it, and angular momentum is angular velocity times moment of inertia. Pull the mass closer to the axis and the moment of inertia drops, so the angular velocity has to rise.
deep: Same trick on ice

The conservation of angular momentum, the Exploratorium notes, explains why ice skaters start to spin faster when they suddenly draw their arms inward, and why divers or gymnasts who go into the tuck position flip or twist at a faster rate.
Moment of inertia
The farther from the axis of rotation the mass is located, the larger the moment of inertia. That is why the bottles start at arm’s length, not against your chest.
Heavier is better
The type of mass is not critical, the Exploratorium says, but two 1-gallon milk jugs full of water work even better than 2-litre bottles. Use the heaviest masses you can hold at arm’s length.

tiles.cap: Two people, one screen, different colours. Sometimes the display is at fault, not the eyes
tiles.nums: types of cone cell in the eye; displays mix red, green and blue to target them, but not everyone’s cones respond the same way
tiles.p1: People perceive colours differently, especially on modern displays that produce a wide range of colours, reports Physics World. Colour vision works thanks to three types of cone photoreceptor cells, and almost all display technologies exploit this by using red, green and blue. The problem with newer displays, Physics World explains, is that they do not necessarily activate the cones of different observers equally. The work was led by Andy Rider of the Institute of Ophthalmology at University College London.
tiles.p2: How it started: Rider says the work began when display technology consultant John Frith got in touch with his group, after a friend of Frith’s in the film industry saw the colours of two side-by-side cinema projectors as wildly different.
deep: Where it is published
The research was led by Andy Rider of UCL’s Institute of Ophthalmology and is published in Optics Express (DOI 10.1364/OE.613255).
Three cones

The three cone types are called L, M and S, and each one responds to different wavelengths of visible light. When two people’s cones differ, the same red, green and blue mix on a display can look different to each of them, what Physics World calls colour mismatches, or metamerism failures.
Test it
Put two phones side by side showing the same photo and ask someone else whether the reds match. If the two of you disagree, the screens may be part of the reason.
tiles.src: Physics World, “Why do people see colours differently? Sometimes, it’s the display’s fault”, Isabelle Dumé, 5 Nov 2026 · Optics Express

tiles.cap: Ant colonies sit still, then all burst into action at once, no leader. A model says why
tiles.nums: scientists have been mystified by the sudden bursts of activity in some ant colonies
tiles.p1: Colonies of some ants sit still for long stretches, then burst into activity all at once with no leader giving the signal; the behaviour has mystified scientists for more than 30 years. Engineers Michael Napoli and Maurizio Porfiri of New York University and biologist Simon Garnier of the New Jersey Institute of Technology built a mathematical model, published on 5 August in PRX Life. In it, one wandering ant bumps a neighbour, which bumps the next, but an ant that has moved must rest before it can be set off again.
tiles.p2: The catch: the first ant can spark activity throughout the rest of its colony only when three conditions line up, how quickly activity can travel through the colony, how easily ants respond to being bumped, and whether the whole colony has switched off into rest mode before the next spark.
deep: Like freezing
The team compares the switch to drastic shifts such as liquid water freezing into solid ice. Once it starts, “like a cascade of dominoes, a massive spike of activity sweeps through the nest.”
Humbling

Kirsten Prior, an ant biologist at Binghamton University who was not involved, says the result suggests bursts come down to simply speed and contact rate, and calls that “a bit humbling to me as an ant biologist.”
Not settled

Grant Navid Doering, a biologist at Bilkent University in Ankara, says experiments with real colonies will be necessary to test the model’s predictions. Elva Robinson, an ecologist at the University of York, says the model opens a “black box” on how bursts happen but not on what colonies gain from them.
tiles.src: Science News Explores, “Mystery solved? Why ‘sleeping’ ants suddenly explode with activity”, Tejasri Gururaj, 6 Nov 2026 · PRX Life, 5 Aug 2026
tiles.credit: Photo: Gilles San Martin (CC BY-SA 3.0), via Science News Explores

tiles.cap: A river that travels 5.5 miles to get 1.3 miles, photographed from the space station
tiles.nums: miles the San Juan River flows (8.9 km) between two points only 1.3 miles (2.1 km) apart
tiles.p1: An astronaut aboard the International Space Station photographed this stretch of the San Juan River in southern Utah on 6 October 2026. The river flows through a series of entrenched meanders, also known as goosenecks, on its westward path to Lake Powell. In Utah’s Goosenecks State Park it runs through a canyon 1,000 feet (300 metres) deep, and one section is so curvy that the river travels 5.5 miles (8.9 km) between two points that are only 1.3 miles (2.1 km) apart.
tiles.p2: Why now: it was NASA Earth Observatory’s Image of the Day for 6 November 2026.
deep: How a river got stuck in rock

Tens of millions of years ago, NASA says, the San Juan shared some characteristics with today’s Mississippi River. Some experts think that, starting around 20 million years ago, the plateau’s rise elevated the river’s headwaters, which increased its gradient and sped its flow. The river cut through 300-million-year-old rock.
The camera

This is astronaut photograph ISS075-E-188830, taken by a member of the Expedition 75 crew with a Nikon Z9 digital camera using a focal length of 400 millimetres. NASA says the image has been cropped and enhanced to improve contrast, and lens artifacts have been removed.
Dark skies

The park’s remote, high-desert location and 360-degree views of the sky helped earn it an International Dark Sky Park designation in 2021. NASA notes that in November 2026 the Northern Taurids, Southern Taurids and Leonids reach their peaks.
Check the ratio
Divide 5.5 by 1.3 and you get about 4.2. On that stretch the water travels more than four times the straight-line distance.
tiles.src: NASA Earth Observatory, Image of the Day for 6 Nov 2026 (story by Lindsey Doermann)
tiles.credit: Photo: NASA / ISS Crew Earth Observations Facility and Earth Science and Remote Sensing Unit, Johnson Space Center

tiles.cap: Your fist at arm’s length covers about 10°: a ruler for anything far away, even the sky
tiles.nums: about the angle your fist covers at arm’s length; an extended hand covers about 20°
tiles.p1: Hold your arm out straight at shoulder height, make a fist and close one eye. The Exploratorium’s rule: measure your arm in fists, thumb not included, and most people come out at a ratio of 1 to 7. Now open your hand and fully extend your fingers. From thumb to little finger, most people’s arms are about three of those long, so whatever you can just hide behind your extended hand is three times farther away from you than it is tall.
tiles.p2: Something to test: stand back from a door until your extended hand, at arm’s length, just covers it: top of the door at the top of your thumb, bottom at the tip of your little finger. Measure how far away you are: it should be about three door-heights.
deep: From ratios to degrees

With both arms outstretched at shoulder level, your arms sweep out 180 degrees. Stack your extended hand from horizon to horizon and you should find about 9 of them fit: 180 ÷ 9 = 20, so your extended hand measures about 20 degrees. About two fists fit in one extended hand, so your fist sweeps out about 10 degrees.
Smaller rulers
The Exploratorium’s table goes on. The width of your thumbnail is about 1:30 of your arm’s length, or 2 degrees. The width of your little fingernail is about 1:60, or 1 degree.
Why it works

When your extended hand just hides a distant object, the object takes up the same angle at your eye as your hand does. Two similar triangles are created, one embedded in the other. The small one has your arm’s length as its base and your hand’s height as its altitude; the large one has the distance to the object as its base and the object’s height as its altitude. Keep your elbow straight: the ratio changes if you bend your arm.
Take it outside

The Exploratorium says this is a tool astronomers use to measure objects in the sky. Mars and Jupiter appear about 1.2 degrees apart before sunrise on 15–16 November: a little more than the width of your little fingernail at arm’s length.
tiles.src: Exploratorium Science Snacks: Handy Measuring Tool · NASA What’s Up, November 2026

tiles.p1: Behavioural scientist Benjamin Lira Luttges at the University of Pennsylvania put it in six words. Do not hand over the things you enjoy and that give you meaning, he says, and decide which skills you want to protect. Trent Cash, a behavioural scientist at the University of Waterloo, adds the mechanism: if we offload a specific skill to AI, we are probably not going to retain that skill particularly well.
tiles.p2: Why it is not scary: Cash also says humans are resilient, and he does not think AI is going to suddenly turn our brains to mush.
deep: The doctors who forgot
Doctors used an AI tool for three months to spot growths during colonoscopies. Back on their own, they did not detect the growths as well.
The readers who gave up

People who used an AI tool to solve SAT questions were more likely to skip questions once the help was removed. The researchers called that particularly concerning, because persistence is key for learning.
Your list
Write down three skills you want to be yours at 20. Those never get outsourced. Everything else is fair game.
tiles.src: Science News Explores, “Is AI making us dumber? Depends how it’s used”, Meghan Rosen, 13 Oct 2026 · Cash et al., Trends in Cognitive Sciences, Aug 2026 · Lira et al., arXiv preprint, Feb 2026
